example: Arguing from the fact that your coffee cools to a purely actual cause is natural theology; citing Genesis 1 as a premise is not.
challenge: Isn't God knowable only by faith, so that reason alone could never reach him?
answer: That is fideism, which Feser explicitly rejects in favor of a rationalist position. Whether reason can reach God is settled by examining the proofs, and many traditions (for instance standard Catholic teaching, as chapter 7 notes) hold that some truths about God are knowable both by reason and by revelation.

example: Aristotle (a pagan), Maimonides (a Jew), Avicenna (a Muslim), Aquinas (a Christian), and Leibniz all offered philosophical arguments for God's existence.
challenge: An appeal to tradition proves nothing, since many people once believed false things.
answer: Agreed, and Feser doesn't use it as proof. It shows only that his confident claim is the historical mainstream rather than an eccentricity, which shifts attention to examining the arguments themselves.

example: From “change occurs,” “a potential is actualized only by something actual,” and “a hierarchical series of actualizers must have a first member,” the existence of a purely actual actualizer is supposed to follow necessarily.
challenge: Metaphysical premises can never be certain; only logic and mathematics give certainty.
answer: Feser argues that some metaphysical premises are certain because denying them is self-defeating. Doubting change is itself a change (chapter 1), and denying PSR undermines all reasoning, including the reasoning behind the denial (chapter 5).

example: Paley: the eye resembles a watch, so it probably had a designer, though evolution might explain it better. Feser: anything with unactualized potential requires something purely actual, and no rival explanation is possible.
challenge: In the end, isn't every argument about reality merely probable?
answer: Not if its premises are certain and its logic valid; then the conclusion is as certain as the premises. Whether a particular proof achieves that is exactly what the book sets out to examine.

example: Against the rationalist proof, saying “maybe the universe is just a brute fact” doesn't count as a refutation; the critic must show that PSR is false or that the argument misuses it.
challenge: Surely a simpler explanation still counts against a theory, whatever kind of argument it is?
answer: Parsimony helps choose between hypotheses that could each be true. If an argument shows no alternative is possible, there is nothing for parsimony to choose between, which is why Feser says the proofs aren't judged by the standards for empirical hypotheses (chapter 7).

example: Arguments for materialism and against free will have many intelligent critics, yet no one concludes they automatically fail.
challenge: If a proof were really sound, wouldn't reasonable people converge on it?
answer: Not necessarily. Feser notes that a demonstration may require substantial philosophical work to defend and that many critics attack caricatures. He also cites Putnam's observation that no argument by even the most celebrated analytic philosophers commands universal assent.

example: Every experiment involves a scientist passing from one observation to another — a change — so no experiment could ever show that change is unreal.
challenge: Couldn't future physics show that change, composition, or contingency are illusions, the way some physicists say the flow of time is?
answer: We can reject particular apparent changes on empirical grounds, but not change as such, because the empirical inquiry would itself be a change (chapter 7). Likewise, science presupposes the intelligibility that PSR expresses (chapter 5).

example: Aristotle's celestial spheres are gone, but the claim that the coffee's potential to cool is actualized by the cool air is untouched by any discovery in astronomy.
challenge: If philosophy can't be tested by experiment, how can it give us knowledge at all?
answer: Science itself rests on philosophical presuppositions it cannot test without circularity: an external world, lawlike regularities, reliable cognition. The claim that only science gives knowledge is not a scientific finding, so scientism refutes itself (chapter 7).

example: A cup is held up by a desk, held up by a floor, held up by a foundation, all at this moment. Or water exists now only because its atoms are bonded in a certain way, which depends on how their particles are arranged.
challenge: Why can't a hierarchical series regress infinitely, just as a linear series might?
answer: Because each member of a hierarchical series has only derived causal power. An infinitely long paintbrush handle still couldn't move itself, and an infinite stack of borrowers never produces a lender (chapter 1).

example: Even if the universe has always existed, the coffee on your desk exists now only because its potential for existence is being actualized now.
challenge: Doesn't the Big Bang show that the universe had a beginning anyway — so why concede a beginningless universe?
answer: Feser thinks it doesn't matter either way. Resting the argument on cosmology would make it hostage to changing science, while the hierarchical argument holds whatever cosmology turns out to be true.

example: God doesn't have wisdom the way Socrates has it, as one feature among others. In God, wisdom, power, and existence are one and the same.
challenge: Isn't this just defining God in a way that conveniently escapes objections?
answer: It is the conception held by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas long before modern debates. More importantly, it is what the proofs conclude to, not an assumption fed into them.

example: Plantinga treats God as having many distinct properties, predicated in the same sense as of creatures, and denies divine simplicity.
challenge: Isn't a personal God exactly what religious believers mean, so that personalism is more faithful to religion?
answer: Classical theists also attribute intellect, will, and love to God. The dispute is over whether God is composite and falls under a genus, and Feser argues that a composite “god” would need a cause and would lack the ultimacy definitive of God (chapter 6).

example: If God's wisdom and power were really distinct parts, something would have to combine them — and that combiner, not “God,” would be ultimate.
challenge: Couldn't there be a composite being that simply exists uncaused, as a brute fact?
answer: The proofs argue that whatever is composite depends on something to account for the combination of its parts (chapter 2). Exempting one composite as a brute fact would also violate PSR (chapter 5).

example: Pure actuality has no parts, so it is simple; what is simple has no essence distinct from its existence; what is subsistent existence itself cannot fail to exist. The five conclusions entail one another.
challenge: Five different arguments might reach five different ultimate beings.
answer: Feser argues, in each Stage 2 and systematically in chapter 6, that there can in principle be only one purely actual, simple being, since nothing could differentiate two of them.

example: Stage 1 of chapter 1 reaches an unactualized actualizer; Stage 2 argues it must be immutable, eternal, immaterial, one, omnipotent, perfect, good, and intelligent.
challenge: Isn't the two-stage structure just a way of organizing chapters rather than part of the argument?
answer: The structure is presentational, but each Stage 2 contains real arguments — for example, uniqueness because nothing could distinguish two purely actual beings — which chapter 6 then develops and defends.

example: Dawkins says there is no reason to credit a first cause with omnipotence or omniscience; chapter 1 argues that pure actuality is the source of all actualizing power and so is omnipotent.
challenge: Even if derivations of the divine attributes exist, they might be weak.
answer: That is a fair line of criticism, but it has to engage the actual derivations of Aquinas, Clarke, and chapter 6. Feser notes that critics like Dawkins and Grayling don't engage them at all (chapter 7).

example: The formal Aristotelian argument's talk of a “first” member makes sense only after the informal discussion explains that “first” means having underived causal power, not being earliest in time.
challenge: If an argument is good, shouldn't its formal version be enough on its own?
answer: The formal steps use technical terms whose meanings are fixed in the informal discussion. Reading them cold invites exactly the misreadings — a temporal regress, “everything has a cause” — that the informal sections are designed to prevent.

example: The proofs can show that God is omniscient, but not that God is a Trinity or inspired the Bible.
challenge: Then isn't the book of little use to religious believers?
answer: No. Establishing one central shared tenet refutes atheism, and chapter 6's account of miracles shows how a revelation could be possible, leaving the question of actual revelation to further inquiry.

example: If the proofs work, a Jewish, a Christian, and a Muslim philosopher still disagree about revelation, but none of their debates starts from “Is there a God?”
challenge: Even granting all of this, couldn't an agnostic simply remain undecided?
answer: Only by identifying some premise or inference to reject. The book's claim is that, when the arguments are examined, every objection to them can be answered; if that is right, remaining undecided is no longer the rational default.
